column5: A location change fires three separate refresh mechanisms at once and revalidates every mounted SWR key including those location cannot affect
column6: onLocationChange at src/helpers/events.ts:45-68 performs three refreshes in sequence for a single user action. It clicks the hidden refetch buttons registered for the current path at :58 - it then calls mutate with a key predicate of () => true at :65 which revalidates EVERY mounted SWR key in the application - and it finally calls updateCartData at :67. The predicate matches indiscriminately so keys that a location change cannot affect are refetched too - orders - notifications - wallet - transactions - profile and the address list. The comment at :64 justifies the overlap on the grounds that SWR dedupes it - but no catalog fetch sets dedupingInterval (issue 36) so the deduping window is the 2 second default - and the button-driven refetches at :58 are explicitly described as covering manual-fetch views which are not SWR keys at all and therefore are not deduped by anything.
column10: Any location or market change through the header selector - including the silent auto-bootstrap on first load when no saved location exists.
column11: 1. Open the app on a screen with several mounted SWR consumers such as the account area. 2. Change the delivery location through the header selector. 3. Watch the network panel and count the requests issued.
column12: One coordinated revalidation of the data that a location change actually invalidates - the catalogue and the cart and settings.
column13: Every mounted SWR key is revalidated plus the path refetch buttons plus a cart refresh so a single location change produces a burst of requests including several for data that cannot have changed.
column14: A request burst against the panel at the exact moment the customer is waiting for the page to settle - worst on slow connections where it delays the content the change was meant to update. The auto-bootstrap path means it can fire on first load without any deliberate user action.
column15: Scope the revalidation to the keys location actually affects rather than a () => true predicate - a market scoped key prefix as issue 35 proposes would make this precise and would also remove the need for the button-click mechanism. Keep one refresh path rather than three.

column5: Every page fetches the settings payload server side on every navigation with no caching
column6: getSettings is called from 28 page files across 56 call sites and every SSR page handler fetches it as part of its getServerSideProps - for example the orders page at src/pages/my-account/orders/index.tsx and the checkout and profile and transactions handlers all do the same. Because these are getServerSideProps handlers they re-run for every client side navigation as well as every full load so each route change issues a fresh settings request. src/services/settings.ts holds no caching of any kind - a search of that file for cache and revalidate and memo returns nothing - and there is no per request memoisation and no shared server side store. CLAUDE.md section 7.3 classifies settings as roughly 30 minute data which is the least volatile category in the table so re-fetching it on every navigation is the furthest departure from the documented policy.
column10: Normal browsing - any navigation between SSR pages which is every page on the site.
column11: 1. Open the site and navigate between five pages. 2. Watch the panel access log or the server side request log. 3. Count the settings requests.
column12: Settings are fetched once and reused for the documented window - through a short lived server side cache keyed by market or a per request memo shared across the handler.
column13: One settings request is issued per navigation per visitor for data that changes about every 30 minutes.
column14: Panel request volume scales with page views rather than with visitors for the least volatile payload in the application - and each fetch sits on the critical path of the server render so it adds latency to every navigation the customer makes.
column15: Add a short lived server side cache for settings keyed by market with a TTL matching the section 7.3 window and read through it from the page handlers. A per request memo would also stop the same handler fetching settings more than once where it does.

column5: The checkout refreshes the cart in its finally block even after the order succeeded and the page has navigated away
column6: The place order handler at src/views/CartPageView/CheckoutSection.tsx:124-156 ends with a finally that runs setLoading(false) and then updateCartData(true - false) at :155. That finally executes on every path including the success path - where the handler has already awaited router.push to either the order detail route or the payment route at :140-146. The cart fetch is therefore issued for a cart the server has just converted into an order while the browser is navigating away from the component that asked for it. updateCartData is called from 31 sites across the codebase and this is the clearest case where the call cannot inform anything the customer sees.
column11: 1. Place an order with any payment method. 2. Watch the network panel through the navigation. 3. Observe the cart request issued after the order call succeeded and the route change began.
column12: The cart is refreshed only where the customer will see the result - on the failure paths where they stay on the checkout screen.
column13: A cart request is issued on the success path too while the page is navigating away.
column14: One wasted authenticated request per order at the busiest moment of the funnel - and it races the navigation so its response is applied to a component that may already be unmounting.
column15: Move the refresh out of the finally and call it only on the failure branches where the customer remains on the checkout screen. The success paths already navigate to a screen that fetches what it needs.
